Language Contact. Occurs when speakers of different languages interact over time, leading to mutual linguistic influence and innovation. Through contact, languages borrow vocabulary, grammar, and sounds. Multilingual speakers develop mixed codes and creoles. Language contact is a primary driver of linguistic diversity and change, reshaping languages and creating entirely new ones throughout history and in the modern world.

Borrowing is the most common contact phenomenon. Words, sounds, or structures from one language enter another. English took "safari" from Swahili and "restaurant" from French. Bilingual speakers mediate contact through their code-switching and interference patterns, which influence both languages over generations. Creoles are new languages that emerge from intense multilingual contact, typically combining grammar from a substrate language with vocabulary from a dominant colonial language. Pidgins are simplified contact languages used for trade or administration. Creoles form when pidgins become native languages to new generations.

Contact can accelerate language change, disrupting normal patterns. Structural simplification often occurs in contact settings. Substratum effects occur when features from suppressed indigenous languages persist in the dominant language of a region. French influence on English after ten sixty-six is a classic example. Prestige asymmetry matters significantly. Borrowing typically flows from high-prestige to low-prestige languages. Language contact threatens endangered languages. Dominant languages often displace smaller ones, and many languages are lost through contact displacement. Mesolectal forms emerge as speakers of different language backgrounds develop intermediate varieties, neither pure source language nor creole. Phonetic accommodation happens in real time. Speakers subtly shift pronunciation toward conversational partners during bilingual interactions. Historical examples illustrate language contact effects. English's enormous French vocabulary after ten sixty-six, Chinese place names absorbed into Japanese, and Hindi-Urdu convergence all demonstrate contact's power. Island languages often illustrate effects of linguistic isolation and contact disruption. Maltese exemplifies intensive contact, blending Romance and Semitic structures and vocabulary. Linguistic isolation is the condition that language contact disrupts and potentially ends. Endangered languages are often threatened by contact with dominant languages. Code switching is the practice through which contact effects emerge in bilingual speakers. Creoles are languages born from contact situations. Sociolinguistics is the field studying language contact in social context. Language change is accelerated and reshaped by contact as part of processes of linguistic evolution. Multilingualism is the personal and societal condition underlying contact effects.
